title: What is the Client Credentials flow — used for machine-to-machine (service-to-service) authentication where there is no user involved — the client sends its own credentials to get a token?
shortTitle: OAuth2 Client Credentials Flow for Machine-to-Machine Authentication

s1_definition.profdef: The Client Credentials flow is the OAuth2 grant used for machine-to-machine authentication, where there is no human user and no delegated access. A confidential client — typically a backend service — authenticates directly to the Authorization Server with its own client_id and client_secret and receives an access token representing the service itself. The token carries the service's own scopes, and the client uses it to call protected APIs. Because no user is involved, there is no consent screen and no refresh token.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India settlement service needs to call the fraud-check service at 2am when no human is around. There is no customer to log in. So the settlement service acts like a staff member with its own employee badge: it shows its own service id and service password to the security office (Authorization Server), receives a work pass (token) stamped with exactly the tasks it is allowed to perform, and uses that pass to enter the fraud-check department. No customer identity is involved — the badge belongs to the service itself.
s1_definition.oneliner: Client Credentials is a service authenticating as itself, with no user and no consent, to call another service.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Client Credentials flow is the OAuth2 grant used for machine-to-machine authentication, where there is no human user and no delegated access. A confidential client — typically a backend service — authenticates directly to the Authorization Server with its own client_id and client_secret and receives an access token representing the service itself. The token carries the service's own scopes, and the client uses it to call protected APIs. Because no user is involved, there is no consent screen and no refresh token.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India settlement service needs to call the fraud-check service at 2am when no human is around. There is no customer to log in. So the settlement service acts like a staff member with its own employee badge: it shows its own service id and service password to the security office (Authorization Server), receives a work pass (token) stamped with exactly the tasks it is allowed to perform, and uses that pass to enter the fraud-check department. No customer identity is involved — the badge belongs to the service itself.

**One line to remember:** Client Credentials is a service authenticating as itself, with no user and no consent, to call another service.

sections.s2_technical:
The flow is a single back-channel call: `POST /token` with `grant_type=client_credentials&scope=fraud:check`, authenticated by the client's own credentials, usually HTTP Basic with `client_id:client_secret` or a signed client assertion. The Authorization Server validates the credentials and the requested scopes against what the client is allowed, then returns an access token. There is no authorization code, no redirect, and no user — because the client is acting on its own behalf, not a user's.

The token is then used exactly like any OAuth2 access token: `Authorization: Bearer ...` on calls to the Resource Server, which validates it and enforces scopes such as `SCOPE_fraud:check`. For example, the Resource Server protects an endpoint with `@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_fraud:check')")` so only services granted that scope can call it. Tokens are short-lived; when one expires the service simply requests another with its credentials — there is no refresh token because there is no user session to keep alive.

The senior points: this flow is only for confidential clients that can protect a secret (never a browser or mobile app). Credentials should come from a secrets manager like Vault, not hardcoded, and should be rotated. Scopes should follow least privilege — the settlement service gets only fraud:check, not account:write. For higher assurance, many banks prefer mutual TLS or signed JWT client assertions over a shared client_secret. The flow is ideal for cron jobs, backend integrations, and microservice-to-microservice calls where no end user is present.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India settlement batch runs overnight and must call the fraud-check service. No customer is logged in, so there is no user token to pass. This is exactly what the Client Credentials flow is for — the service authenticates as itself.

Problem 2 — Even a trusted internal service must not be all-powerful; the settlement service should be able to call fraud-check but not, say, close accounts. This is exactly why the token carries scopes — least privilege confines the service to only what it needs.

Our mini-project builds an `AuthorizationServer` that issues a token to a service presenting valid client credentials and allowed scopes, and a `ResourceServer` (fraud-check) that enforces the scope. The demo shows the settlement service getting a token and calling fraud-check successfully, then being refused when it requests a scope it is not allowed, and a service with a wrong secret being refused a token.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run
javac ClientCredentialsDemo.java
java com.bank.clientcred.ClientCredentialsDemo

# Spring Boot
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/oauth2-client-credentials-service-1.0.0.jar

# Fetch a machine-to-machine token (no user)
curl -X POST https://auth.nationalbank.example/token \
  -d 'grant_type=client_credentials&scope=fraud:check' \
  -u 'settlement-service:correct-secret'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the settlement-service client with secret correct-secret, requesting scope fraud:check, then a transaction TXN-9001 for 95000.

Step 1: The settlement service calls the token endpoint with its own client id and secret and the requested scope. No user is involved and there is no redirect — this is a pure back-channel machine call.

Step 2: The Authorization Server validates the credentials and checks the requested fraud:check against the client's allowed scopes. Both pass, so it issues a short-lived access token carrying scope fraud:check that represents the service itself.

Step 3: The settlement service calls the fraud-check Resource Server with the token. The Resource Server confirms the token carries fraud:check and runs the check on the 95000 transaction, returning REVIEW because it exceeds the 90000 threshold.

Step 4: When the settlement service requests account:close, the Authorization Server refuses at the token endpoint because that scope is not in its allowed set, enforcing least privilege. When a wrong secret is presented, the Authorization Server refuses to issue any token at all.

```text
2026-10-31 23:25:00.010 INFO    [ClientCredentialsDemo] Settlement service obtained M2M token with scopes: fraud:check
2026-10-31 23:25:00.012 INFO    [ClientCredentialsDemo] Fraud-check responded: REVIEW
2026-10-31 23:25:00.013 SEVERE  [ClientCredentialsDemo] Scope refused at token endpoint: client not allowed scopes: [account:close]
2026-10-31 23:25:00.014 SEVERE  [ClientCredentialsDemo] Client auth failed: invalid client credentials for settlement-service
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Settlement Service (no user)        Authorization Server        Fraud-Check API
         │                                   │                          │
         │ POST /token grant=client_credentials                          │
         │  id+secret + scope=fraud:check    │                          │
         │──────────────────────────────────▶ validate creds + scope    │
         │◀──────── access token ────────────│                          │
         │ GET /check (Bearer m2m-token) ───────────────────────────────▶ scope ok
         │◀─────────────── verdict REVIEW ───────────────────────────────│
    wrong secret → no token ; disallowed scope → refused at /token
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Client Credentials (M2M) ═══

  ┌──────────────────┐ client_credentials ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ Settlement Svc   │────────────────────▶│ Authorization Server│ issue service token
  │ (confidential)   │◀────service token───│ (validate id/secret)│
  └────────┬─────────┘                     └─────────────────────┘
           │ Bearer token (scope=fraud:check)
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────────┐  validate token + scope
  │ Fraud-Check Service │── fraud:check  → allow
  │ (Resource Server)   │── account:*    → deny
  └─────────────────────┘
  secret stored in Vault; NO user, NO consent, NO refresh token
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Client Credentials flow ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   AuthorizationServer    │        │     FraudCheckServer      │
  │ ──────────────────────── │        │ ───────────────────────── │
  │ - clients: Map<id,       │        │ + check(token,txn,amt):   │
  │     {secret, scopes}>    │        │     String                │
  │ ──────────────────────── │        │   throws InsufficientScope│
  │ + tokenForClient(id,     │        └───────────────────────────┘
  │     secret, scopes):Str  │
  │   throws ClientAuthException
  └──────────────────────────┘

  Contract for tokenForClient(id,secret,scopes):
    Pre:  id known, secret matches
    Post: token with requested scopes IF subset of allowed
    Throws: ClientAuthException on bad secret OR disallowed scope
  No user / no consent / no refresh; least-privilege scopes; secret from Vault
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Client Credentials flow is the OAuth2 grant for machine-to-machine authentication, where there is no human user and no delegated access. A confidential client, typically a backend service, authenticates directly to the Authorization Server with its own client id and client secret and receives an access token that represents the service itself. The token carries the service's own scopes, and because no user is involved there is no consent screen and no refresh token.

In my banking project the overnight settlement batch needs to call the fraud-check service when no customer is logged in. There is no user token to pass, so the settlement service authenticates as itself with its own credentials, requests the fraud:check scope, and receives a short-lived token. It then calls the fraud-check API with that token exactly like any bearer token, and the fraud-check service enforces the scope.

The least-privilege point is central. In my demo the settlement service is allowed fraud:check and nothing else, so when it tries to request account:close the Authorization Server refuses at the token endpoint. And when a wrong secret is presented, no token is issued at all. This keeps even trusted internal services confined to exactly what they need.

The nuances I always raise are that this flow is only for confidential clients that can protect a secret, never a browser or mobile app, that the secret must come from a secrets manager like Vault and be rotated rather than hardcoded, and that for higher assurance banks often prefer mutual TLS or signed JWT client assertions over a shared secret. Client Credentials is the right tool for cron jobs, backend integrations, and microservice-to-microservice calls where there is simply no end user.

---

keyPoints: OAuth2: delegated authorization — app accesses user data on their behalf
Authorization Code Flow: safest for web apps — code exchanged server-to-server
PKCE: extra security for mobile/SPA — no client secret needed
OIDC: authentication layer on top of OAuth2 — ID token with user info
